title: Kicker Candle
teaches: The Kicker as we trade it: a leader already set up, a real red day that closes weak at support, then a day that gaps up at least 1.5%, trades through the red day's high and never fills the gap; the buy is a market order over the red high on the Kicker day (never the close), the stop a few cents under the Kicker day's low or 3.5% under the entry if closer, a third off at 3R and 5R, and a stop-out is the plan working.

steps: BBY, 2013. A leader coils in a 6.2% range. The red day, down 1.8%, closes at 2% of its range.

Closes at 99% of its range, up 15.1%. 3R on day 1: a third off, stop to breakeven. Another third at 5R.

questions.q: Which pair of candles is a Kicker?
choices: Weak red day, then a gap over its close
Green day, then red under its low
A doji, then a small inside day
Two red days that each gap lower
questions.answer: Weak red day, then a gap over its close
questions.why: A weak red day, then a gap up that trades through its high. The red day is a real drop that closes weak near its low at support, like a failed breakdown. The Kicker day then gaps up at least 1.5%. It trades through the red day's high and never trades back to the red close. A baby red candle or a doji does not count.
questions.lesson_line: A Kicker is a failed breakdown followed by a gap that traps the sellers.

wrong.Green day, then red under its low: That is a drop after strength. A Kicker is a red day, then a gap up.
wrong.A doji, then a small inside day: A doji or a baby candle traps nobody, and an inside day has no gap.
wrong.Two red days that each gap lower: Gaps down are the opposite. The Kicker day gaps up.

questions.simple: A Kicker is a weak red day at support followed by a gap up that trades through the red high.

reasons: names the proposed 1.5% gap line
rests on the house card plus one public UCT definition

questions.q: A Kicker can follow a baby red candle or a doji.
questions.why: False. The red day must close below its open and look like a breakdown that traps sellers. A baby red candle or a doji is not it. With nobody trapped there is no kick, so a gap after one is a plain breakout. GWW is the case: a red body of 0.04% of price and a drop of 0.4%, then a 2.2% gap.
questions.lesson_line: No trapped sellers, no kick. After a baby candle it is a plain breakout.
questions.simple: A baby red candle or a doji traps no sellers, so a gap after it is a plain breakout.

reasons: settled card criterion, two agreeing house facts

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The Kicker day gaps up at least ___%.
questions.why: 1.5%. The Kicker day gaps up at least 1.5%. A smaller gap does not count.
questions.lesson_line: A Kicker gaps up at least 1.5%.
questions.simple: The gap must be at least 1.5%. A smaller gap does not count.

reasons: the 1.5% line is a proposed card threshold, not yet an owner ruling

questions.q: On the Kicker day, where is the buy trigger?
choices: One cent over the red day's high
The Kicker close, at market
A cent under the red day's low
A cent over the red day's open
questions.answer: One cent over the red day's high
questions.why: One cent over the red day's high, on the Kicker day only. It is a market buy as the stock trades through that price. The close is too late: buying the close is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the red high. The close is too late.

wrong.The Kicker close, at market: Buying the close is a named mistake. The entry is the trade through the red high.
wrong.A cent under the red day's low: We buy over the red high, not under the red low.
wrong.A cent over the red day's open: The trigger is the red day's high, not its open.

questions.simple: We buy at market one cent over the red day's high as it trades through. Never at the close.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling of 2026-11-02 for the Kicker entry

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The buy over the red high is a market order on the ___ day only.
questions.why: Kicker. Entry A is a market buy one cent over the red day's high, on the Kicker day only. If the day opens above that price, the fill is at the open. The trigger does not carry to a later day.
questions.lesson_line: The red-high trigger works on the Kicker day only.
questions.simple: The buy happens on the Kicker day only, the day the stock trades over the red day's high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (entries are market orders)
fixed before

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The Kicker stop sits a few cents under the Kicker day's ___.
questions.why: Low. The stop sits a few cents under the Kicker day's low, not exactly on it. If 3.5% under the entry is closer, use that.
questions.lesson_line: Stop under the Kicker day's low, or 3.5% under the entry if that is closer.
questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the Kicker day's low, or 3.5% under the entry if that is closer.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62 and the 2026-11-02 Kicker stop ruling)

questions.q: In a Red market, a Kicker long waits while we stay mostly in cash.
questions.why: True. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. A Kicker long needs a Green or Yellow reading, or Orange for an A+. A bounce in a Red market looks like a Kicker and is not. Red still allows shorts below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Check the market first. In a Red market the Kicker waits.
questions.simple: True. In a Red market we stay mostly in cash, so a Kicker long waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (market reading, F65 and D46)
fixed before

questions.q: What does 'the gap holds' mean on the Kicker day?
choices: It stays over the red day's close
It closes above its open
It opens over the red day's high
It holds above the 50-day
questions.answer: It stays over the red day's close
questions.why: It stays over the red day's close. The gap holds when the Kicker day never trades back down to that close. If it does, the gap has filled and the Kicker is off. Where the day opens against the red high is not the test.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fills is not a Kicker. Hold above the red close or walk away.

wrong.It closes above its open: The test is the red close, not the open. A gap can hold on a day that fades.
wrong.It opens over the red day's high: That is where it opens, not what holds. The gap holds if it never trades back to the red close.
wrong.It holds above the 50-day: The 50-day is context before the red day. The gap holds against the red close.

questions.simple: The gap holds when the stock never trades back down to the red day's close.

reasons: gap-holds is a proposed card criterion
fixed before

questions.q: Where does a Kicker belong?
choices: On a base or an orderly pullback
After a vertical run with no base
Under a falling 200-day
On any earnings gap
questions.answer: On a base or an orderly pullback
questions.why: On a base or an orderly pullback. The leader is already set up: tight closes before the red day, held above its 200-day, with the 50-day flat or rising. A stock mid-run with no base is not a setup, and a gap right after a report is an earnings gapper.
questions.lesson_line: No base, no setup. The Kicker sits on top of a leader that is already set up.

wrong.After a vertical run with no base: A stock mid-run has no base, so it is not a setup.
wrong.Under a falling 200-day: No longs below the 200-day, except a parabolic long.
wrong.On any earnings gap: The first session after a report is mostly an earnings gapper, a PEG.

questions.simple: A Kicker sits on a stock that is already set up, in a base or an orderly pullback.

deeper.trap: On 2011-08-03 IDCC looked like a Kicker: red day -5.8%, gap 5.7%, +13.8% on 2.7x. But the prior 20 closes spanned 44.1% after a 60% burst, so there was no base. It was taken anyway and stopped the next session at 0.0R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-025, the earnings-day Kicker)
fixed before

questions.q: The textbook bullish kicking pattern is a bearish candle, a gap up, then a bullish candle.
questions.why: True. Bulkowski's strict form is a tall black marubozu, an upward gap, then a tall white marubozu. Schwab gives the same order and says neither candle has shadows. Our Kicker is looser than this textbook shape.
questions.lesson_line: Textbook kicking is shadowless. Ours is a real red day, a gap and context.
questions.simple: True. Schwab and Bulkowski both list a bearish candle, a gap up, then a bullish candle, and Schwab says neither has shadows.

deeper.counter: Our Kicker is not the textbook candle. Our card wants a real red day that closes weak near its low at support. Then the Kicker day gaps up at least 1.5%, trades through the red day's high and never fills the gap.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree; both quotes re-opened and found on their pages 2026-11-11

questions.q: What is the Kicker stop cap?
choices: 3.5% under the entry price
3% under the entry price
5.5% under entry price
The low of the base
questions.why: 3.5% under the entry price. The Kicker keeps its own cap of 3.5%, not the usual stop of about 3%. If the honest stop is more than 3.5% away, it is not a clean Kicker. The cap is a ceiling: a Kicker day low that sits closer sets the stop instead.
questions.lesson_line: The Kicker cap is 3.5%. A wider honest stop means pass.

wrong.3% under the entry price: That is the usual rule of thumb for stops. The Kicker keeps 3.5%.
wrong.5.5% under entry price: That is wider than the cap. A stop that wide means it is not a clean Kicker.
wrong.The low of the base: The base low can be far away. The stop sits under the Kicker day.

questions.simple: It is 3.5% under the entry. A stop that must be wider than that means the trade is not a clean Kicker.

reasons: rests on the owner's Kicker stop ruling (3.5% cap)

questions.q: A Kicker is about positioning and is rarely an earnings day.
questions.why: True. Our card says the Kicker is rarely an earnings day and is about short-term positioning. If the gap day is the first session after a report, the card grades it as an earnings gapper, a PEG, and not as a Kicker.
questions.lesson_line: Kickers are positioning. The day after a report belongs to the earnings gapper.
questions.simple: True. A Kicker is about short-term positioning, and a gap right after a report is an earnings gapper instead.

deeper.counter: LUV, 2026-01-29, passed the shape tests: a weak red day, a gap and a strong close out of a base. But the gap day was the earnings reaction day, after a report on 2026-01-28. So it is graded as a Power Earnings Gap, not a Kicker.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-025, the earnings-day Kicker)
fixed before

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A base or an orderly pullback: the last 20 closes span ___% or less of price.
questions.why: 15%. A base or an orderly pullback means the last 20 closes span 15% or less of price. A wider span is not a base.
questions.lesson_line: Twenty closes inside a 15% span: that is the base.
questions.simple: The last 20 closes must span 15% or less of price, which marks a tight base.

deeper.trap: The span is a share of price, not dollars. A stock mid-run that spans far more than 15% is not a base, however tidy the last candle looks.

reasons: the 15% span is a proposed criterion value that may change

questions.q: Where should the red day end?
choices: At support, like the 21 or 50-day
At a fresh 52-week high
In free fall, far from averages
Near its high, after a dip
questions.why: At support, like the 21-day or 50-day. The card says the red day ends at support: its close within 1.5 ATR of the 21-day EMA or the 50-day SMA, or at or under the lowest low of the prior 5 sessions plus 1%. A drop into a level traps the sellers who sold the break. The red day also closes weak, near its low.
questions.lesson_line: The red day falls into a level. That is what makes the gap a trap.

wrong.At a fresh 52-week high: That is a breakout, not a breakdown. Nobody sold a break, so nobody is trapped.
wrong.In free fall, far from averages: A shock-day red bar looks like a Kicker and is not. It is not an orderly pullback into a level.
wrong.Near its high, after a dip: The red day closes weak, near its low. A strong close near the high traps no sellers.

questions.simple: The red day must end at a support level, like the 21-day or 50-day, so the sellers get trapped.

reasons: the support thresholds are card numbers that may change
fixed before

questions.q: A bearish engulfing candle after your Kicker buy is not a sell signal.
questions.why: True. After entry we do not sell early on a next-day gap back, a bearish engulfing candle or a close back under the red day's high. The stop is the exit for a failed trade. A close under the red high on the Kicker day is a warning for the grade, not an exit. Planned trims at 3R and 5R, and the trail on the last third, are part of the plan, not early exits.
questions.lesson_line: A candle is not an exit. The stop is.
questions.simple: True. After you buy, the stop ends a failed trade, so a scary candle is not a reason to sell.

deeper.example: On 2023-03-16 PGR was bought. On day 2 it closed back under the red high, and the stop traded the same day. The stop did the work, not the candle.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)
fixed before

questions.q: What floor must a stock clear before we buy a Kicker?
choices: $10 a share and $20 million a day
$15 a share, $50 million a day
$2 a share and $10,000 a day
A strong leader can skip it
questions.answer: $10 a share and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million a day. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. The app detector's floor is far lower, $2 and $10,000 a day, so an alert alone does not clear ours.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars a share, twenty million a day. Below that, no Kicker.

wrong.$15 a share, $50 million a day: Too high. Our floor is $10 a share and $20 million a day.
wrong.$2 a share and $10,000 a day: That is the app detector floor, far under ours. Our floor is $10 and $20 million.
wrong.A strong leader can skip it: Every setup has the floor. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.

questions.simple: Our floor is $10 a share and $20 million traded a day, so thin stocks are not even watched.

deeper.trap: The trap is the app's alert. The detector's floor is $2 and $10,000 a day, so it can fire on a stock we would never watch. Check our own $10 and $20 million floor before you plan the buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: If the 3.5% stop is too wide for your risk, move the stop closer until the size fits.
questions.why: False. Size comes from the stop, never the reverse. Set the stop first, a few cents under the day's low. Shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade. A stop tightened to fit is not the honest stop.
questions.lesson_line: Never fit the stop to the size. Fit the size to the stop, or skip.
questions.simple: False. The stop is set first from the chart, then you size to it, and if it does not fit, you skip.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)

questions.q: How much comes off at the first trim, 3R?
choices: A third
Half
All of it
A quarter
questions.why: A third. The hard rule is a third off at 3R. After that comes another third at 5R and a trail on the last third, and that part is adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: A third comes off at 3R. That is the hard rule.

wrong.Half: The hard rule is a third, not half.
wrong.All of it: The hard rule trims a third at 3R, not the whole position.
wrong.A quarter: The hard rule is a third at 3R.

questions.simple: A third comes off at 3R. That is our hard rule for the first trim.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51: a third at 3R is the hard rule)

questions.q: Owning 5% of a stock's average daily volume is within our limit.
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. No setup lifts that cap. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the stock too. One percent of its daily volume is the ceiling.
questions.simple: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: Bought at 48.60 with the stop at 47.40. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 52.20. One R is the fill minus the stop, the risk on each share. Add three of those to the fill: 48.60 + 3 x (48.60 minus 47.40) = 52.20. The first third comes off there.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: Take the fill minus the stop, multiply it by three, and add that to the fill price.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (a third off at 3R)

questions.q: Which red day sets up the better Kicker?
choices: Closes near its low, at the 21-day
Closes mid-range, at the 21-day
Closes near its high, at the 21-day
Closes near its open, a tiny body
questions.answer: Closes near its low, at the 21-day
questions.why: Near its low, at support. The red day is a real drop that closes weak, like a failed breakdown. The sellers who sold the break are trapped. Support means near the 21-day or 50-day average, or at a recent low. A mid-range close does not look like a breakdown: our example, ISRG, is a regular gap up.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close at support sets the trap. A mid-range close is a regular gap up.

wrong.Closes mid-range, at the 21-day: A mid-range close does not read as a failed breakdown. Our ISRG example is a regular gap up.
wrong.Closes near its high, at the 21-day: A close near the high is not a breakdown, so nobody is trapped.
wrong.Closes near its open, a tiny body: A close near the open is a baby red candle. Nobody is trapped, so there is no kick.

questions.simple: The best red day is a real drop that closes weak near its low at support, which traps the sellers.

deeper.example: BBY, 2013: a 6.2% tight range into the 21-day EMA and the 50-day. The red day fell 1.8% and closed at 2% of its range. Next morning it gapped up 2.1% and the gap held, and it closed up 8.8%.

reasons: the red-day close cutoff is a held decision (D-097), so no number is taught
support test is a proposed card criterion
fixed before

questions.q: A Kicker can also be bought on a break of the first 30-minute high of the Kicker day.
questions.why: True. Entry B is the opening-range break on the Kicker day: a buy-stop one cent over the high of the first 30-minute bar. Entry A, one cent over the red day's high, is the other entry. Pick one price and one stop, because we buy once. The first bar is only 30 minutes long, even on a 60-minute chart.
questions.lesson_line: Two entries: over the red high, or over the first 30-minute high.
questions.simple: True. Entry B buys one cent over the high of the first 30-minute bar on the Kicker day.

reasons: which 30 minutes counts is a held decision (D-031)

questions.q: The red day closed at 44.10. The Kicker day opens at 44.75. What is the gap, as a percent of the red close, to two decimals?
questions.why: 1.47%. The gap is the open minus the red day's close, over that close: 44.75 against 44.10. The Kicker day must open at least 1.5% above the red day's close, so 1.47% is just short. Rounding it to 1.5% would hide that.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap. A gap a hair short of the line is not a gap.
questions.simple: The gap is 1.47%, which is under the 1.5% line, so this is not a Kicker gap.

deeper.example: On 2024-06-10 CEG opened 0.8% over the red close, short of the 1.5% line. The red day was -2.3% and the stock rose 8.4% on 2.0x volume. With no real gap it was a plain breakout day, a strong green bar, not a Kicker.

reasons: a computed key
the 1.5% line is a proposed criterion value

questions.q: Where is the buy?
choices: 27.97, a cent over the red high
27.96, right at the red high
27.95, a cent under the high
The Kicker close at market
questions.story: The red day's high is 27.96. The next morning the stock gaps up 2.1% but opens under that high, then trades up through it.
questions.answer: 27.97, a cent over the red high
questions.why: 27.97. The buy is one cent over the red day's high of 27.96, filled at market as the stock trades through it. This stock opened under that high, so the order waited. BBY was bought the same way on 2013-07-01 at 27.97.
questions.lesson_line: Buy one cent over the red high as it trades through.

wrong.27.96, right at the red high: The order sits one cent over the high, not on it.
wrong.27.95, a cent under the high: That is under the high, before the stock has traded through it.
wrong.The Kicker close at market: Never at the close. The trigger is the trade through the red high.

questions.simple: We buy at market one cent over the red high, 27.96, as the stock trades through it. That price is 27.97.

deeper.example: BBY, 2013-07-01: the red day closed at 2% of its range, the Kicker day gapped 2.1% and the gap held. The buy was 27.97, a cent over the red high. It closed up 8.8% at 92% of its range.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling of 2026-11-02 for the Kicker entry
key is a price worked out one cent over the story's high

questions.q: Where does your first stop go?
choices: 59.83, 3.5% under the fill
61.85, just under the red high
No stop until 10:00, then 3.5%
Under the red day's low
questions.story: The red high was 61.90. The Kicker day opens over it, and you are filled at the open at 62.00. The day has no low yet.
questions.why: 59.83. A fill at the open has no Kicker low yet, so the first stop is 3.5% under the fill: 62.00 x 0.965 = 59.83. At 10:00 it is raised to a few cents under the 30-minute low if that is higher. It is a real stop order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: No low yet means 3.5% under the fill. Raise it once the low exists.

wrong.No stop until 10:00, then 3.5%: Every position has a real stop order from the start. At 10:00 it only moves up.
wrong.Under the red day's low: The stop sits under the Kicker day's low, not the red day's. With an open fill there is no Kicker low yet, so it starts 3.5% under the fill.
wrong.61.85, just under the red high: The red high is the trigger. The first stop on an open fill is 3.5% under the fill.

questions.simple: With no low yet, the first stop goes 3.5% under your fill, and it moves up later.

deeper.example: COHR, 2024-01-16: the Kicker opened 0.2% over the red high, so the fill came at the open, 42.83. With no low yet, the first stop was 3.5% under the fill, 41.33. At 10:00 it could rise to the 30-minute low if that was higher.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's ruling (stop on an open fill)
fixed before

questions.q: Filled at 27.98. The Kicker day's low so far is 26.90. Where is the stop?
questions.why: 27.00. Two stops compete: a few cents under the 26.90 low so far, or 3.5% under the 27.98 fill, which is 27.00. Take the one closer to the entry. The low-based stop sits under 26.90, so it is farther away. The 3.5% stop is the closer one.
questions.lesson_line: Two stops, one answer: take the one closer to the entry.
questions.simple: The stop is 27.00, because 3.5% under the fill is closer than a few cents under the low.

deeper.trap: The trap is anchoring on the low. A few cents under 26.90 feels safe, but it is farther from the 27.98 fill than 3.5% is, so it would risk more than the cap. The stop closer to the entry wins.

reasons: a computed key (3.5% under the fill)
rests on the owner's rulebook (Kicker stop ruling, F62)

questions.q: The buy point is 83.20. The Kicker opens at 86.00. How far above the buy point is that, in percent, to one decimal?
questions.why: 3.4%. Take the open minus the buy point, over the buy point: 86.00 against 83.20 is about 3.4%. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, so this open is inside the limit. Past 4%, the open is a chase. A morning flush that curls back up is another way in.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the open against your buy point. Past 4% over it, you are chasing.
questions.simple: The open is 3.4% over the buy point, under the 4% chase limit, so it is not a chase.

reasons: a computed key
the 4% chase limit is the owner's rulebook (C28); the flush way in is the owner's ruling D-022

questions.q: Can you buy the open?
choices: No; over 4% above the buy point
Yes, a gap up shows strength
Yes, with a smaller stop
No; it opens over the red high
questions.story: The red high is 50.00, so your buy point is 50.01. The Kicker day opens at 52.60.
questions.answer: No; over 4% above the buy point
questions.why: No. The open, 52.60, is more than 4% above the 50.01 buy point. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. A gap up is not a reason to chase. A morning flush that curls back up is another way in.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4% over the buy point, the open is not ours. A morning flush that curls up can be.

wrong.Yes, a gap up shows strength: Strength is not a reason to chase. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
wrong.Yes, with a smaller stop: You do not tighten the stop to fit. The stop stays put and the distance grows.
wrong.No; it opens over the red high: Opening over the red high is allowed. A market buy fills at the open. The block is the 4% limit.

questions.simple: No, because the open is more than 4% above the buy point, and we never chase.

reasons: the 4% no-chase limit is the owner's rulebook (C28); the flush way in is the owner's ruling D-022

questions.q: Which of these ends the trade before you buy?
choices: It trades back to the red close
It gaps up 2.4% on heavy volume
It trades over the red day's high
It opens under the red day's high
questions.answer: It trades back to the red close
questions.why: It trades back to the red day's close. That fills the gap before the trigger, so there is no trade. The Kicker also needs a trade over the red day's high, which is the trigger itself. A gap of 1.5% or more is what you want, and a filled gap is what kills the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A filled gap is a dead Kicker. Walk away.

wrong.It gaps up 2.4% on heavy volume: A gap of 1.5% or more is what you want. A filled gap is what kills it.
wrong.It opens under the red day's high: Opening under the red high does not end it. The buy-stop one cent over the red high simply waits until the stock trades through.

questions.simple: If the stock trades back down to the red day's close, the gap has filled and there is no trade.

reasons: inverse-gap criterion is a proposed card rule

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, a report is inside 3 sessions
Yes, it is a Kicker, not earnings
No, it is really an earnings gapper
Yes, then sell before the report
questions.story: A clean Kicker triggers over the red high. The company reports earnings in two sessions.
questions.answer: No, a report is inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 sessions before an earnings report, and a report in two sessions is inside that window. The rule bars the buy itself. A clean Kicker is not exempt, and a plan to sell before the report is still a new buy.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.

wrong.Yes, it is a Kicker, not earnings: The report window is its own rule and the Kicker does not escape it.
wrong.Yes, then sell before the report: The rule is no new buys inside the window, not buy and run.
wrong.No, it is really an earnings gapper: The earnings gapper is the first session after a report. This report is still two sessions away, so the block is the 3-session window.

questions.simple: No, because a report is two sessions away, and we buy nothing new in the 3 sessions before a report.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean Kicker. It can look perfect and still sit inside the window. GOOGL on 2020-02-03 reported after the Kicker's own close and gapped down the next morning. AVGO on 2024-03-07 did the same. Check the calendar before the buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, the 3-day earnings window)

Move it to breakeven, 42.00
Lower it for more room

Sell it all at the close, it failed
Move the stop up to breakeven now
Add on the dip to lower the cost

questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. Only the stop sells you.

wrong.Sell it all at the close, it failed: A close under the red high is a warning for the grade, not an exit.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven now: Our plans move the stop to breakeven at the first trim, not on a weak close.

100.00, the stop as it was
Out at once, the loss is past 2R
The open, 98.50, the gap price

questions.why: 98.20. A gap down through the stop hands the decision to the first 30 minutes, and the low of that first 30-minute bar is the new stop. Here that low is 98.20. The loss at that low is inside the 2R ceiling, so we stay in. Only a loss past 2R in the first 30 minutes means get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Out at once, the loss is past 2R: The loss at the 30-minute low is inside the 2R ceiling.
wrong.The open, 98.50, the gap price: The open is not the decision. The 30-minute low is.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the gap price as the stop. The open at 98.50 is only the first print. The rule waits for the first 30 minutes, uses the low of that bar, and gets out only if that loss is past 2R.

questions.q: Do you buy the close?

Yes, a strong close confirms
No, buy tomorrow's open
Yes, with the 3.5% stop

questions.q: Fill 55.00. The 10-day average is 49.00. How far above the 10-day is the fill, in percent, to one decimal?
questions.why: 12.2%. The gap is the fill minus the 10-day average, over that average: 55.00 against 49.00 is about 12.2%. We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average, so we pass on this one. The test uses the 10-day average as the base, not the fill.
questions.lesson_line: Too stretched to buy: skip a long more than 10% over its 10-day.
questions.simple: The fill is 12.2% above the 10-day average, past the 10% limit, so we skip it.

deeper.counter: Two tests can disagree. The 4% chase limit measures the fill against the buy point. The 10% stretch test measures the fill against the 10-day average. A buy can pass one and fail the other, and it must pass both.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

questions.q: In our rule, the Kicker gap is measured from which price?
choices: The red day's close
The red day's open
The red day's high
The red day's low
questions.why: The red day's close. Our Kicker day opens at least 1.5% above the red day's close. Bigalow compares the second open with the prior day's open instead. The red high is the trigger, not the start of the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap from the red close, not the open.

wrong.The red day's open: Bigalow compares the opens. Ours is the red close.
wrong.The red day's high: The red high is the trigger, not the start of the gap.
wrong.The red day's low: The low is not a gap reference.

questions.simple: The gap starts at the red day's close, so the Kicker day must open at least 1.5% above it.

deeper.counter: Bigalow's page says the second candle opens at the same open as the previous day, or gaps open. He compares opens. Ours is measured from the red day's close, and it must be at least 1.5%.

reasons: rests on our criteria card (proposed 1.5% gap) and differs from Bigalow's version

questions.q: Filled at 22.17 with the stop at 21.76. How far under the fill is the stop, as a percent of the fill, to one decimal?
questions.why: 1.8%. The stop distance is the fill minus the stop, over the fill: 22.17 against 21.76 is about 1.8%. That is inside the Kicker's 3.5% cap, so the stop passes that test. If the honest stop is more than 3.5% away, it is not a clean Kicker.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop. Over 3.5% away, it is not a clean Kicker.
questions.simple: The stop is 1.8% under the fill. That is inside the 3.5% cap, so the stop passes the cap test.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's ruling (the 3.5% cap)

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 0.5%. Fill 22.17, stop 21.76. How many shares, rounded down? The position cap does not bind.
questions.why: 1219 shares. Risk dollars are 100,000 x 0.5%. Divide that by the stop distance, 22.17 minus 21.76, and round down to 1219. The size is the smaller of this and the position cap, and the cap does not bind here. The stop comes first and sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then size. Shares are risk dollars over the stop distance.
questions.simple: Divide the money you risk by the gap between fill and stop, then round down to whole shares.

deeper.trap: If the honest stop does not fit your risk, you skip the trade. You never tighten the stop to make the size bigger. The stop comes first, the size comes from it, and the smaller of the risk-based size and the position cap sets the shares.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5)

Sell it all, bank the 3R gain

Hold all, nudge the stop up

questions.lesson_line: At 3R sell a third and lift the stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell half, keep the same stop: The hard rule is a third, and the stop moves up at the first trim.
wrong.Hold all, nudge the stop up: The first third comes off at 3R.

questions.simple: Sell a third and move the stop to breakeven, because 23.40 is 3R and the hard rule trims a third there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19) and the 2026-11-02 trade plan

Trim later, at the close

Add a third; the gap shows strength

Widen the stop to give it room

questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R: sell and use the money elsewhere.

wrong.Add on a breakout of the range: We buy once, and a slow trade is not a reason to add.
wrong.Hold; the stop is untouched: A trade under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, even though the stop has not been hit.

wrong.No, sell it all while it is strong: The plan sells a third at 3R and another third at 5R, then trails the last third. It does not sell it all on a push.

A red-to-green at the open

Hold, the base is still intact
Buy it back at the next open

wrong.Move the stop under the base low: A stop never moves down or wider.
wrong.Hold, the base is still intact: The stop is the exit. It is not a debate.
wrong.Buy it back at the next open: After a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger.

questions.simple: Take the loss, because the stop is the exit, and buy again only if a new trigger appears.

deeper.trap: The trap is hope. The chart looked textbook: an 8.1% base, a red day on its low, a 1.7% gap. The next day's low was 175.34, under the 177.50 stop. The stop makes the loss small, and a new buy needs a new trigger.

Proved the setup was a bad one

questions.simple: The stop did its job and kept the loss to the plan, while the close under the red high was only a warning.

deeper.trap: The trap is selling at the close because it sits under the red high. Our card calls that a warning for the grade, not an exit. Here the stop at 137.35 traded the same day anyway, and the stop is the exit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4) and one card line on the warning

No stop until the close
Under the red day's low

Locked in a loss on the whole trade

Take it; the gap is all that counts

questions.q: Does the base pass our checklist?
questions.story: A leader's last 20 closes span 12%, so the base looks tidy. Up close, its daily bars are wide and stacked over one another. Yesterday was a weak red day.
choices: No; wild, overlapping bars fail it
Yes; the 12% span is what counts
No; a 12% span is too wide for a base
Yes; wide bars show strong demand

questions.why: No. The span test is only part of our checklist: the last 20 closes span 15% or less, and 12% passes that. The checklist also wants no wild, overlapping bars in the base. Wide bars that overlap wildly make a sloppy base, and a tidy 20-close span does not hide them.

Yes, buy the 49.70 high on the fade

questions.simple: True. The trigger is a trade above the red day's high, and a gap up alone does not fire it.
